rows.selection_reason: With no prior evidence, the first experiment should establish a strong reference point for the core multimodal hypothesis. config_002 pairs the most expressive encoders in each modality (scgpt for RNA, ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L for images) with transformer-based aggregation (more expressive than avgpool for combining multiprofile outputs) and standard concat fusion. This tests whether the full multimodal pipeline with learned, non-linear components in both branches can achieve high validation accuracy. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can ablate individual components (encoder choice, aggregation, fusion) to identify what drives performance. If it underperforms, it signals that complexity in one or more components is the bottleneck, guiding targeted follow-ups. This is the highest-information single experiment under a 10-run budget because it simultaneously validates the multimodal architecture, the encoder choices, and the aggregation strategy.

With only one data point (config_002: multimodal, scgpt+ViT-L, transformer+concat → acc 0.507, F1 0.455), the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodality is actually contributing value or whether a single modality can achieve comparable performance. Config_014 (image_only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool) uses the same image encoder and profile setting as config_002, providing a clean ablation: if image-alone accuracy is near 0.507, RNA is not adding signal and we can focus experiments on image-side optimizations; if it is substantially lower, multimodality is confirmed as important and we should invest remaining budget in optimizing the fusion and RNA encoder. This single experiment resolves a binary strategic question that would otherwise consume multiple experiments to answer indirectly, making it the highest-information use of experiment 2 with 8 remaining.

Evidence: config_002 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat) achieved 0.507 accuracy, far exceeding image-only config_014 (0.332), confirming multimodal fusion is essential. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt) and don't know whether the RNA representation quality is a bottleneck. Question: config_019 changes only the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), and fusion (concat) identical to config_002. This clean one-variable comparison isolates the RNA encoder's contribution. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is a fundamental design choice that determines the quality of the transcriptomic representation fed into fusion. With 7 experiments remaining, establishing whether scgpt or scvi_n200 is superior early will guide all subsequent multimodal experiments and prevent wasting budget on suboptimal encoder combinations. If scvi_n200 matches or exceeds scgpt, it opens a large branch of configurations; if scgpt is clearly better, we can confidently exploit scgpt-based variants.

Evidence: config_019 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat, multiprofile) achieved 0.721 accuracy, far surpassing config_002 (scgpt variant, 0.507) and config_014 (image-only, 0.332), establishing scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation as the strongest backbone. Question: config_008 is a single-variable perturbation of config_019, changing only the fusion strategy from concat to weighted while keeping scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, and multiprofile fixed. This tests whether learned weighted fusion (which can down-weight a noisier modality) outperforms simple concatenation. Why best next: With 6 experiments remaining, exploiting the clear winner by probing the most impactful remaining design axis (fusion) is the highest-information use of this slot. A positive result would immediately yield a new best; a negative result confirms concat and redirects effort to aggregation or image-encoder variations.

Evidence: The two best experiments (config_008: 0.725, config_019: 0.721) both use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation, with only a marginal difference between weighted and concat fusion. The RNA encoder (scvi_n200 >> scgpt) and aggregation (transformer) are well-supported, but the image encoder has only been tested as imagenet_vit_l. Question: Does swapping the image encoder to resnet50 (a CNN vs ViT architecture) maintain or improve performance? config_013 is a clean single-variable change from the best config (config_008), isolating the image encoder effect. Why this is the best use: With 5 experiments remaining, confirming or ruling out the image encoder as a performance lever is critical—if resnet50 matches or beats ViT-L, we gain flexibility for later fine-tuning; if it underperforms, we lock in imagenet_vit_l and can focus remaining budget on subtler hyperparameters (aggregation, fusion, profile setting).

Evidence: The top three experiments (config_008: 0.725, config_019: 0.721, config_013: 0.713) all use scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation, with weighted fusion and imagenet_vit_l as the best combination. However, we have not yet tested whether transformer aggregation is truly necessary versus simpler avgpool when paired with the best RNA encoder and image encoder. This experiment (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) isolates the aggregation variable while holding all other components at their best-known settings. If avgpool matches transformer (~0.725), it confirms the architecture is robust and frees us to explore other dimensions (e.g., singleprofile, different encoders) in the remaining 4 experiments. If avgpool is significantly worse, it confirms transformer is a critical component and we should focus remaining budget on fusion/image-encoder refinements around the transformer backbone. This is the highest-information experiment because it reduces uncertainty on a key architectural choice with a clean one-variable comparison.

The current best (config_008, 0.725 acc) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. The RNA encoder is the most impactful design choice (scvi_n200 ≈ 0.72 vs scgpt ≈ 0.51), but pca_n2000 has never been tested in any multimodal setting. Config_034 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) isolates the RNA encoder variable while holding all other hyperparameters at their empirically best values, directly testing whether a simpler linear PCA representation could match or exceed the generative scvi model. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-value experiment: if pca_n2000 is competitive, it opens a new optimization axis for the remaining 3 experiments; if not, it confirms scvi_n200 is optimal and we can focus remaining budget on fine-grained refinements around the current best.

The top three results (config_008: 0.7250, config_019: 0.7207, config_013: 0.7131) all use multiprofile with scvi_n200, confirming scvi_n200 as the dominant RNA encoder and transformer+weighted as the best aggregation/fusion pairing. However, the singleprofile dimension remains completely untested across all 7 completed experiments. Config_031 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile, weighted) pairs the two best-performing encoders with the best fusion strategy in the unexplored singleprofile architecture. This is the highest-information experiment available: if singleprofile is competitive, it opens a new design axis for the remaining 2 experiments; if it underperforms, it firmly confirms multiprofile as the superior architecture and lets us focus the final budget on fine-tuning the multiprofile winner. With only 2 experiments left, reducing uncertainty on this major untested design choice is more valuable than a small incremental test within the already well-characterized multiprofile space.

The current best is config_008 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725). The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion. The only untested combination in this top-tier region (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer) is config_004 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat). While weighted > concat and imagenet_vit_l > resnet50 in prior tests, testing this configuration completes the 2x2 image-encoder × fusion matrix within the transformer-aggregation, scvi_n200, multiprofile subspace. If it underperforms as expected, it confirms config_008 as the optimal configuration with high confidence before the final experiment. If it unexpectedly performs well, it provides a new candidate for the last experiment. This is the best use of experiment 9 because it reduces residual uncertainty in the most promising region with minimal risk, leaving the final experiment free to either confirm or fine-tune the best configuration found.

The best result so far is config_008 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725). The evidence strongly indicates that scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l are the optimal encoders, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion are optimal, and multiprofile is essential. Among untested multiprofile scvi_n200 configs, config_050 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) retains both top encoders and represents the closest untested variant to the best configuration, differing only in aggregation and fusion. While unlikely to surpass 0.725 given the consistent performance gaps (transformer>avgpool by ~0.019, weighted>concat by ~0.004), it has the highest expected accuracy among remaining candidates and provides a final confirmation of the ranking of aggregation/fusion choices under the optimal encoder pair. As the last experiment, it maximizes the probability of confirming or marginally improving upon the current best.
